Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)

claims.text: Qualifying furniture and fittings expenditure is capital expenditure incurred on furniture and fittings, including those used in vessels, ships, aircrafts, trains, plants, and buildings, for the purposes of trade or business.
In Table I, Furniture and Fittings Expenditure is in Class 2, with a rate of 20%.

Where a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business, an allowance (capital allowance) at the rate specified in Table I is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for the purposes of that trade or business.
Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately.
A capital allowance for an asset is made for a year of assessment if, at the end of a basis period, the person is the owner of the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business.

The residue of a qualifying expenditure at any date is the total qualifying expenditure incurred on or before that date for the asset, less the total capital allowance made for that asset before that date.

An allowance shall not be made for a year of assessment unless it is claimed for that year, or where the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so.

Where an allowance is not claimed in the year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for the purposes of the trade or business, it shall be carried forward to a subsequent period.

The allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the relevant year of assessment, and any part that cannot be fully deducted for lack of remainder is treated as a deduction for the next year and succeeding years until fully utilised.

claims.text: Input VAT is the VAT a taxable person pays to a supplier on a taxable supply made to that person.
Output VAT is the VAT a taxable person collects on making taxable supplies.

Where output VAT exceeds input VAT, the taxable person must remit the excess to the Service not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.
Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, the taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months.
Input tax may be deducted only to the extent it was incurred for the purpose of consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.
Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s73(1)-(4): advance rulings on application by a taxable person, issued within 21 days or with written reasons.
cases.question: Can my company ask the tax service for a written ruling on how a law applies before we go ahead with a deal?

claims.text: An advance ruling may be issued for clarity, consistency and certainty on how any tax law is interpreted and applied, as long as it does not amount to an amendment or replacement of the law.
The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling upon application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give reasons in writing for being unable to issue it.
An application is made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to a tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more parties to it.

An advance ruling covers any written opinion or decision given to a taxpayer by the relevant tax authority on a transaction, proposed transaction or any tax matter, to give direction or clarification.

The application must contain the taxpayer's contact details, a complete description of the issue or transaction and its financial implications, if any, and a complete description of its impact on the tax liability of the taxpayer or any connected person.

The application must also give details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and decisions of the tax authority on the issue, the statutory provisions or legal basis relied on, the reasons the ruling should be granted, and a written statement on whether the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction.

The relevant tax authority may request additional information from an applicant and, where necessary, shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or provide clarifications.
An applicant may withdraw an application at any time before a ruling is issued.

The relevant tax authority may reject an application where it requires an opinion, conclusion or determination on the laws of a foreign country, an issue already before a court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, the interpretation of the Constitution, an issue that is academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious, or a ruling that will interfere substantially with an ongoing audit, investigation or other proceeding involving the applicant or persons connected to the applicant.
The effect of a ruling is limited to the applicant and the transaction for which it is given, and it is rendered on a set of facts before the tax authority and cannot be of general application.

An advance ruling is void where the transaction actually carried out is materially different from the one described, where there is fraud, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact, or where an assumption made or condition imposed by the tax authority is not satisfied or carried out by the taxpayer.

An advance ruling ceases to be effective where the tax law provision it concerned is repealed or amended in a way that materially affects it, from the date the repeal or amendment takes effect, or where a court overturns or modifies the interpretation it is based on, from the date of the judgement unless that decision is overturned.

gaps: The passages do not say what the prescribed form and manner of application is.
The passages do not say whether the company counts as a taxable person or a party to the deal, which depends on its facts.

claims.text: Every person, including a company granted exemption from incorporation, shall maintain books or records of accounts, whether or not the person is liable to pay tax.
The books and records required to be maintained shall be in English language and, for the purpose of tax, shall be consistent with the format that may be prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where the record is maintained in a language other than the English language, the person shall, on demand by the tax authority, produce at its own expense a translation in English language which shall be certified by a sworn translator.

A taxable person who fails to keep accounts, books and records of business transactions and income, to allow for the correct ascertainment of tax and filing of returns to the relevant tax authority, is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 in the case of a company.
A taxable person who, upon request by the relevant tax authority, fails to provide any record or book prescribed in the Act is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 in the case of a company.

The word "book" includes any register, document or other records of information and any account or accounting record, however compiled, recorded or stored, including in written, printed, micro-film, digital, magnetic or electronic form or otherwise.

gaps: The passages do not say whether keeping records in French, with an English translation produced on demand, counts as keeping books in the English language for the penalty in section 102.
The passages do not say whether the company is a taxable person or what format the relevant tax authority has prescribed.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares a dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act.
The charge is made as if the dividend is the total profits of the company for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
This applies whether or not the recipient of the dividend is a Nigerian company.
The charge does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent that the profits or gains in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act.
The charge does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
The charge does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

The charge does not apply to distributions by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods.

gaps: The rate prescribed in section 56 is not among the passages, so the rate and the tax amount cannot be stated.
The meaning of franked investment income is not in the passages.

Whether the company's own situation (for example, whether its profits are exempt or its earnings were already taxed) falls within an exception needs facts about the company that the passages do not give.

claims.text: Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess tax as a credit against subsequent months. This applies not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require.
Input VAT is the VAT a taxable person pays to a supplier on a taxable supply made to the person.
Output VAT is the VAT a taxable person collects on making taxable supplies.

Input tax on a taxable supply to a registered person may be deducted from the tax payable on its taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.
Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

gaps: Whether the purchases in question were made for making taxable supplies, and whether they were made after the Act commenced, is not stated.
The actual due date for the return is set in the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, which is not among the passages.

claims.text: Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the appointed person has failed to collect the VAT.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and who was issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under that section is to be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction, or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remittance is to be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

A person with an obligation to collect VAT under Chapter Six shall keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances. The compliance provisions apply to that person as though it were the taxable person.

gaps: Whether the foreign online company is a non-resident person, and whether the software services are taxable supplies, is not stated in the passages.
Whether the Service has appointed this supplier to collect VAT is not stated in the passages.
Whether the payer is a taxable person is not stated in the passages.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": A small business has gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less in the cited print and ₦50,000,000 or less in the Gombe print. (DR-267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": Total fixed assets must be less than ₦250,000,000 in the cited text and not more than ₦250,000,000 in the National Assembly text, so exactly ₦250,000,000 qualifies only under the National Assembly text. (DR-270)

claims.text: Under the definition of connected persons, a company is connected to another company where the same person has control over both companies, or connected persons acting separately have control over the companies.
Two companies are also connected where one company participates directly or indirectly in the management, control or capital of the other company.
Two companies are also connected where the same persons participate directly or indirectly in the management, control or capital of a company and another company.

In other cases, two persons are connected where one may reasonably be expected to act in accordance with the directions, requests, suggestions or wishes of the other, or both may reasonably be expected to act that way for a third person, or one has the practical ability to control the business decisions of the other.
Two persons are not connected solely because one is the employee or client of the other, or both are employees or clients of a third person.
Related parties has the same meaning as connected persons.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company or the Nigerian permanent establishment of a non-resident company incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purpose of Chapter Two of the Act.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is above 30% of the Nigerian company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation in that accounting period.
The Schedule's limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted in an assessment year is carried forward to following assessment years and allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule.
Interest expenditure shall not be carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.
The deduction for interest on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.

For the Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, where the tax audit commenced before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit in subsection (1), where there is a deliberate misstatement by a taxable person in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as may be necessary, assess the taxable person to the amount or additional amount necessary to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.

All relevant facts are to be considered in computing the additional amount of tax, even where those facts were not known when a prior assessment or additional assessment was made for the taxable person in the same year.

The tax authority is not prevented from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year if it does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that was determined for that year under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

gaps: Whether a given case involves a deliberate misstatement is not answered by the passages.
The passages do not say how the six years are counted for a particular filing date; that date calculation is not done here.

claims.text: Where a business produces no assessable profit, or an assessable profit less than expected from that business, or where the true amount of the assessable profit cannot be readily ascertained, the relevant tax authority may act under section 38.

In the case of a resident, the relevant tax authority may assess and charge the taxable person on such fair and reasonable percentage of the gross income from the trade or business as the relevant tax authority may determine.
In the case of a non-resident, the profits are the amount resulting from applying the profit margin of the person to the turnover generated from Nigeria.

For this purpose, profit margin is the proportion of Earnings Before Interest and Tax to income or revenue in the published audited financial statement of the business. For persons not required to publish financial statements, it is the profit margin the relevant tax authority may ascertain from financial statements of comparative companies.

claims.text: Subject to section 11 of the Act, where a taxable person has given notice of an objection or appeal, collection of tax stays in abeyance until the objection or appeal is determined.
The taxable person shall pay the tax that is not the subject of the objection or appeal.

Tax charged by an assessment that is not or has not been the subject of an objection or appeal is payable within 30 days of service of the notice of assessment, and the relevant tax authority may in its discretion extend the time for payment.

Once an objection or appeal is determined, the relevant tax authority shall serve a notice of the tax payable as determined, and that tax is payable within 30 days of the date of service of that notice.
Where there is no objection or appeal, the relevant tax authority may proceed to enforce recovery of the tax payable in accordance with the Act.

A valid objection must be delivered to the relevant tax authority within 30 days from the date of service of the disputed notice of assessment, and it must contain the grounds of objection listed in section 41(2)(b).
The relevant tax authority may, for satisfactory and good cause shown, extend the time for making the objection to such reasonable time in the particular circumstances.

gaps: Section 11 of the Act, to which the rule on holding back collection is subject, is not among the passages.
Which part of a particular assessment is disputed and which part is not is not stated, so the amount to be paid cannot be worked out.

claims.text: Where a valid VAT refund request is received from a taxable person, the Service shall, not later than 30 days of receiving the request, refund the tax to the taxable person, or the amount shall be eligible for set-off against any tax liability of the taxpayer.
A taxable person that qualifies for a VAT refund shall make the request to the Service in the prescribed form.
The request shall be made not later than 12 months after the transaction giving rise to the refund, otherwise it shall lapse.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require.

gaps: The passages do not say how the 30 days are counted or what happens if the Service does not pay within that time.
The passages do not say whether the general tax refund timeline of 90 days in the Tax Administration Act section 55 applies to VAT refunds as well as the 30 days.

claims.text: Section 192 deals with transactions between related parties, which must be at arm's length.
A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length.
A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party which is not at arm's length, the authority may make necessary adjustments to bring it into line with arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations.
The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192.
For section 192, an "arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions.
For section 192, "arm's length terms and conditions" means terms and conditions obtainable if the transaction or arrangement was between unrelated parties dealing in comparative circumstances.
The adjustment power in section 192 is stated to be as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations.

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company, at 0% for a small company.
Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.
Where a company's effective tax rate in a year of assessment is less than 15%, it shall recompute and pay additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%.
That 15% rule applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

gaps: The passages do not define a small company, so whether the company is one cannot be told.
The company's total profits after losses and capital allowances are not known, so the tax cannot be worked out from the profit figure given.
Whether the company is an MNE group member or has the turnover that triggers the 15% rule is not stated.
The calculation of the tax amount is not done here.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

claims.text: Qualifying furniture and fittings expenditure is capital expenditure incurred on furniture and fittings, including those used in vessels, ships, aircrafts, trains, plants, and buildings, for the purposes of trade or business.
In Table I, Furniture and Fittings Expenditure is in Class 2, with a rate of 20%.

Where a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business, an allowance (capital allowance) at the rate specified in Table I is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which that asset was used for the purposes of that trade or business.
Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately.
The allowance is made for a year of assessment if, at the end of a basis period, the person is the owner of the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business.

An allowance is not made for a year of assessment unless the person claims it for that year, or the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so.
Where an allowance is not claimed in the year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for the purposes of the trade or business, it is carried forward to a subsequent period.

The allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the relevant year. Where the remainder is nil or insufficient, the part not yet deducted is treated as a deduction for the next year and succeeding years until fully utilised.

The residue of a qualifying expenditure at any date is the total qualifying expenditure incurred on or before that date for the asset, less the total capital allowance made for that asset before that date.

A notional 1% of qualifying capital expenditure is recorded in the capital allowance computation schedule for statistical purposes until the asset is disposed of. It does not increase or reduce the capital allowance claimable.

claims.text: A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on a taxable supply made to the person, and that VAT is known as input VAT.
A taxable person collects VAT on making taxable supplies, and that VAT is known as output VAT.

Where output VAT exceeds input VAT, a taxable person shall remit the excess to the Service not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.
Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months.

Input tax on a taxable supply may be deducted from tax payable on taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.

Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred, and the deductible input tax is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s73(1)-(4): advance rulings on application by a taxable person, issued within 21 days or with written reasons.
cases.question: Can my company ask the tax service for a written ruling on how a law applies before we go ahead with a deal?

claims.text: An advance ruling may be issued to give clarity, consistency and certainty on how any tax law is interpreted and applied, as long as it does not amount to an amendment or replacement of the law.

The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling upon application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give reasons in writing for being unable to issue the ruling.
An application is made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to a tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more parties to it.

An advance ruling includes a written opinion or decision given to a taxpayer by the relevant tax authority on a transaction, a proposed transaction or any tax matter, to provide direction or clarification.

An application must contain the taxpayer's name, Tax ID, postal address, email address and telephone number, and a complete description of the tax issue or transaction, including its financial implications, if any.

An application must also describe the impact on the tax liability of the taxpayer or any connected person, give details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and decisions on the issue, and state the statutory provisions or legal basis relied on and the reasons the ruling should be granted.
An application must also include a written statement on whether or not the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction.

The relevant tax authority may request additional information from an applicant and, where necessary, shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or provide clarifications.
An applicant may withdraw an application at any time before a ruling is issued.

The relevant tax authority may reject an application where it requires an opinion, conclusion or determination on the laws of a foreign country, an issue already before a court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, the interpretation of the Constitution, an issue that is academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious, or a ruling that will interfere substantially with an ongoing audit, investigation or other proceeding involving the applicant or connected persons.
A ruling is limited in effect to the applicant and the transaction for which it is given, and it is rendered on a set of facts before the tax authority and cannot be of general application.

A ruling is void where the transaction actually carried out is materially different from the one described, where there is fraud, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact, or where an assumption made or condition imposed by the tax authority is not satisfied or carried out by the taxpayer.

A ruling ceases to be effective where the tax law that was its subject is repealed or amended in a way that materially affects it, or where a court overturns or modifies the interpretation on which it is based.

gaps: The passages do not say which body counts as the relevant tax authority for a particular company's deal.
The passages do not state the prescribed form and manner for applications.

cases.question: We have just started a poultry farming company. Is there an income tax exemption for new agricultural businesses?

claims.text: Income generated by companies engaged in agricultural businesses is exempt from tax under Chapter Two of the Act. The exemption covers crop production, livestock, aquaculture, forestry, dairy and such other businesses as described in the Thirteenth Schedule, for the first five years upon commencement of business.
The Thirteenth Schedule lists livestock activity as raising and breeding of animals in ranches and farms, and also lists livestock processing.

gaps: The passages do not say that poultry farming counts as livestock or as an agricultural business under the exemption.
The passages do not say how commencement of business is determined for the five-year period, or whether the exemption has further conditions elsewhere in the Act.
The Thirteenth Schedule passage prints no exempted products, so it does not say whether any product is named for poultry.

Income generated by companies engaged in agricultural businesses is exempt from tax under Chapter Two of the Act. The exemption covers crop production, livestock, aquaculture, forestry, dairy and such other businesses as described in the Thirteenth Schedule, for the first five years upon commencement of business. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 163(1)(m) to (v); Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 163(1)(a) to (c)]

The Thirteenth Schedule lists livestock activity as raising and breeding of animals in ranches and farms, and also lists livestock processing. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Thirteenth Schedule, Exemption for agricultural businesses]

- The passages do not say that poultry farming counts as livestock or as an agricultural business under the exemption.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 163(1)(m) to (v) (gazette page A 478)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 163(1)(a) to (c) (gazette pages A 476, A 477)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Thirteenth Schedule, Exemption for agricultural businesses (gazette page A 593)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 163(1)(m) to (v): The gazette exempts a Nigerian company's profits from goods or services exported from Nigeria (other than petroleum companies) if the export proceeds are repatriated through official channels; the National Assembly text has no such exemption. (DR-074)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Thirteenth Schedule, Exemption for agricultural businesses: The gazette's 'EXEMPTED PRODUCTS' column is empty. The National Assembly text populates the exempted products for each activity, adds the sub-sector name for 'Cocoa processing', and adds an 'Animal feeds' row. (DR-178)

claims.text: Every person, including a company granted exemption from incorporation, shall maintain books or records of accounts, whether or not the person is liable to pay tax.

The books and records required to be maintained under subsection (1) shall be in English language and shall, for the purpose of tax, be consistent with the format that may be prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where the record is maintained in a language other than the English language, the person shall, on demand by the tax authority, produce at its own expense a translation in English language which shall be certified by a sworn translator.

A taxable person who fails to keep accounts, books and records of business transactions and income, to allow for the correct ascertainment of tax and filing of returns to the relevant tax authority, is liable to an administrative penalty, which for a company is ₦50,000.
A taxable person who, upon request by the relevant tax authority, fails to provide any record or book prescribed in the Act is liable to an administrative penalty, which for a company is ₦50,000.

"Book" includes any register, document or other records of information and any account or accounting record however compiled, recorded or stored, whether in written or printed form or micro-film, digital, magnetic or electronic form or otherwise.

gaps: The passages do not say whether keeping records in French, with an English translation produced on demand, counts as meeting the English language requirement or avoids the penalty in section 102.
The passages do not say what format the relevant tax authority has prescribed.

claims.text: A development levy of 4% is imposed on the assessable profits of all companies chargeable to tax under Chapters Two and Three of the Act, other than small companies and non-resident companies.
A small company is therefore outside the companies on which the development levy is imposed under that section.
A small company means a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000.
Any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company, so it is not excluded from the levy as a small company.

gaps: Whether a particular company meets the small company definition depends on its own turnover, fixed assets and type of business, which the passages do not state.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax.

The charge is at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act, as if the dividend were the total profits of the company for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
This applies whether or not the recipient of the dividend is a Nigerian company.
The charge does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent that the profits or gains included in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act.
The charge does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
The charge does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

The charge does not apply to distributions made by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods.

gaps: The rate in section 56 is not among the passages, so the rate that applies is not stated.
The meaning of franked investment income is not in the passages.
Whether the company's own facts fall within an exception, and the resulting tax amount, would need a calculation and facts not given.

claims.text: Gains accruing to an individual are exempt from tax on the disposal of a dwelling-house or part of it, or an interest in it.
The exemption also covers land immediately adjoining the dwelling house, up to a maximum of one acre, but not land used for commercial purposes.
The exemption under this section shall be enjoyed once in the lifetime of an individual.

Where a person disposes of only a part of a dwelling-house, or of a house used partly as a dwelling place and partly for carrying out a trade, business, profession or vocation, the consideration shall be apportioned.

claims.text: Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess tax as a credit against subsequent months. This is to be done not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of the information or documents the Service may require.
Input VAT is the VAT a taxable person pays to a supplier on taxable supplies made to that person.
Output VAT is the VAT a taxable person collects on making taxable supplies.

Input tax on a taxable supply to a registered person may be deducted from the tax payable on its taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.
Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

gaps: Whether the reader's purchases and sales are taxable supplies, and whether the reader is a taxable or registered person, is not stated.
The amount of any credit or refund would need a calculation from the reader's figures.

claims.text: Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the appointed person has failed to collect the VAT.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under this section shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service.

The remission must be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

A person with an obligation to collect VAT shall keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances, and the compliance provisions apply to that person as though it is the taxable person.

gaps: Whether the software services are taxable supplies is not stated in the passages.
Whether the foreign online company is a non-resident person, or has been appointed by the Service to collect VAT, is not stated in the passages.
Whether the payer is a taxable person is not stated in the passages.

A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person does not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the appointed person has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under this section shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

The remission must be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

A person with an obligation to collect VAT shall keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances, and the compliance provisions apply to that person as though it is the taxable person. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

- Whether the software services are taxable supplies is not stated in the passages.
- Whether the foreign online company is a non-resident person, or has been appointed by the Service to collect VAT, is not stated in the passages.
- Whether the payer is a taxable person is not stated in the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151 (gazette pages A 472, A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155 (gazette page A 474)

The return of a small company may contain a statement of accounts attested to by the taxpayer in place of audited financial statements.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": A small business has gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less in the cited print and ₦50,000,000 or less in the Gombe print. (DR-267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": Total fixed assets must be less than ₦250,000,000 in the cited text and not more than ₦250,000,000 in the National Assembly text, so exactly ₦250,000,000 qualifies only under the National Assembly text. (DR-270)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)

claims.text: In the case of a company, a company is connected to another company where the same person has control over both companies, or connected persons acting separately have control over the companies.
Two companies are also connected where one company participates directly or indirectly in the management, control or capital of the other company.
Two companies are also connected where the same persons participate directly or indirectly in the management, control or capital of a company and another company.

In other cases, two persons are connected where one may reasonably be expected to act in accordance with the directions, requests, suggestions, or wishes of the other, or both may reasonably be expected to act that way for a third person, or one has the practical ability to control the business decisions of the other.
Two persons are not connected solely because one is the employee or client of the other, or both are employees or clients of a third person.
"Related parties" has the same meaning as connected persons.

claims.text: Interest paid on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is a deductible expense, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.

Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purposes of Chapter Two.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is above 30% of the Nigerian company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation in that accounting period.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted in an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule.
Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.

Under the Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.

gaps: The passages do not say whether a sister company is a connected person, so whether the limit applies to this loan is not stated.
The passages do not give the company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation or the interest paid, so the actual limit in naira is a calculation that is not done here.

claims.text: Subject to the Act, any tax law or regulation, a company that has been in business for more than 18 months must file its return not more than six months after the end of its accounting year.
Every company must file a self-assessment return with the Service in the prescribed form at least once a year, with or without notice from the Service, whether or not it is liable to pay tax.

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, where the tax audit commenced before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit in subsection (1), where there is a deliberate misstatement by a taxable person in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as may be necessary, assess the taxable person to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.

All relevant facts are to be considered in computing the additional amount of tax, even where those facts were not known when a prior assessment or additional assessment was made for the taxable person in the same year.

The tax authority is not prevented from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year that does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that was determined for that year under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

gaps: The passages do not say whether a return filed for a year counts as an assessment for the purpose of the six years, or from what date the six years run in a particular case.

A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length.

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%.
Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains computed in accordance with Part VIII of Chapter Two, less the amount of any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6), and capital allowance in accordance with Part I of the First Schedule.
Where a company's effective tax rate in a year of assessment is less than 15%, the company shall recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%.
That 15% rule applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.
Dividends received by a Nigerian company by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax under the Act.

gaps: The passages do not say whether the company is a small company, so the applicable rate cannot be picked.
The question does not say whether the ₦120 million is total profits after losses and capital allowances, so the tax base is not known.
The question does not say whether the company is in an MNE group or has the turnover that triggers the 15% effective tax rate rule.

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s73(1)-(4): advance rulings on application by a taxable person, issued within 21 days or with written reasons.
cases.question: Can my company ask the tax service for a written ruling on how a law applies before we go ahead with a deal?

claims.text: An advance ruling may be issued for clarity, consistency and certainty on how any tax law is interpreted and applied, provided it does not amount to an amendment or replacement of the law.

The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling upon application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give reasons in writing for being unable to issue the ruling.
An application is made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to any tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more parties to it.
An advance ruling covers a transaction, a proposed transaction or any tax matter, and is given in writing as an opinion or decision to direct or clarify.
An application must contain the taxpayer's name, Tax ID, postal address, email address and telephone number.

An application must also contain a complete description of the issue or transaction, including its financial implications if any, and of its impact on the tax liability of the taxpayer or any connected person.

An application must also contain details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and decisions of the tax authority on the issue, the statutory provisions or legal basis relied on, and the reasons why the ruling should be granted.
An application must also contain a written statement on whether or not the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction.
The tax authority may request additional information from an applicant.
Where necessary, the tax authority shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or provide clarifications.
An applicant may withdraw an application at any time before a ruling is issued.

The tax authority may reject an application where it requires an opinion, conclusion or determination on the laws of a foreign country, an issue already before a competent court or tribunal, or the interpretation of the Constitution.

The tax authority may also reject an application on an issue that is academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious, or on a ruling that will interfere substantially with an ongoing audit, investigation or other proceeding involving the applicant or persons connected to the applicant.
A ruling's effect is limited to the applicant and the transaction for which it is given, and it is rendered on the set of facts before the tax authority and cannot be of general application.

An advance ruling is void where the transaction actually carried out is materially different from the one described, where there is fraud, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact, or where an assumption or condition set by the tax authority is not satisfied or carried out by the taxpayer.

claims.text: Every person, including a company granted exemption from incorporation, shall maintain books or records of accounts, whether or not the person is liable to pay tax.
The books and records required to be maintained shall be in English language and shall, for the purpose of tax, be consistent with the format that may be prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where the record is maintained in a language other than English, the person shall, on demand by the tax authority, produce at its own expense a translation in English language certified by a sworn translator.

A taxable person who fails to keep accounts, books and records of business transactions and income, to allow for the correct ascertainment of tax and filing of returns, or who fails on request to provide any record or book prescribed in the Act, is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 in the case of a company.

"Book" includes any register, document or other records of information and any account or accounting record, however compiled, recorded or stored, including in written, printed, micro-film, digital, magnetic or electronic form.

gaps: Whether keeping accounts in French, with an English translation produced only on demand, counts as failing to keep books under the penalty provision is not stated in the passages.
Whether the company is a taxable person for the penalty provision is not stated in the passages.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act.
For that charge, the dividend is treated as the total profits of the company for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
This rule applies whether or not the recipient of the dividend is a Nigerian company.
The rule does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent that the profits or gains in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act.
The rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
The rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

The rule does not apply to distributions made by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods.

claims.text: Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess tax as a credit against subsequent months. This applies not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require.
VAT paid by a taxable person to a supplier on a taxable supply made to the person is called input VAT.
VAT collected by a taxable person on making taxable supplies is called output VAT.

Input tax on a taxable supply, including services and fixed assets, may be deducted from the tax payable on taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies.
Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to making taxable supplies may be deducted.
Input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

claims.text: Under the definition of connected persons, a company is connected to another company where the same person has control over both companies, or connected persons acting separately have control over the companies.
Two companies are connected where one company participates directly or indirectly in the management, control or capital of the other company.

Two persons are not connected solely because one is the employee or client of the other, or both are employees or clients of a third person.
Related parties has the same meaning as connected persons.

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for Chapter Two purposes.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is more than 30% of the Nigerian company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation in that accounting period.
Interest on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is a deductible expense, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company that is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Interest expenditure that is not wholly deducted for an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted under paragraph (2) of the Schedule.
Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately after the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.

For the Schedule, debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.
A deduction is not allowed for any payment to a connected person that is not consistent with the Transfer Pricing Regulations issued by the Service.

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment where the tax audit began before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit in subsection (1), where a taxable person makes a deliberate misstatement in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the taxable person for the amount needed to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.

All relevant facts are to be considered in computing the amount or additional amount of tax that should have been charged, even where those facts were not known when a prior assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year.

The tax authority may make an assessment or additional assessment for a year if it does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that was determined for that year under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

gaps: The passages do not say from what date the six years run beyond the words "within six years of the assessment", and the exact end date would need a calculation.

claims.text: Subject to section 11 of the Act, collection of tax where the taxable person has given notice of an objection or appeal remains in abeyance until the objection or appeal is determined.
The taxable person must still pay the tax that is not the subject of an objection or appeal.

A written notice of objection is valid only if delivered to the relevant tax authority within 30 days from the date of service of the disputed notice of assessment, and it contains the grounds of objection listed in the section; the authority may extend this time for satisfactory and good cause shown.

claims.text: Section 192 deals with transactions between related parties, which must be at arm's length.
A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length.
A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party that is not at arm's length, the authority may make necessary adjustments to bring it in line with arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations.
The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192.
For section 192, an "arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions.
For section 192, "arm's length terms and conditions" means the terms and conditions obtainable if the transaction or arrangement was between unrelated parties dealing in comparative circumstances.
Section 192 makes the tax authority's adjustment power subject to the Transfer Pricing Regulations, and it also refers to rules or regulations the relevant tax authority may make.

A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party that is not at arm's length, the authority may make necessary adjustments to bring it in line with arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

For section 192, an "arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

For section 192, "arm's length terms and conditions" means the terms and conditions obtainable if the transaction or arrangement was between unrelated parties dealing in comparative circumstances. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Section 192 makes the tax authority's adjustment power subject to the Transfer Pricing Regulations, and it also refers to rules or regulations the relevant tax authority may make. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The text of the Transfer Pricing Regulations is not among the passages.
- The definition of "related party" is not among the passages.
- Any rules or regulations made under section 192 and the prescribed form and manner of reporting are not among the passages.
- The meaning of "relevant tax authority" is not among the passages.

Sources

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company, at 0% for a small company.
Tax on any other company is levied at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less the amount of any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.
A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source.
Dividends received by a Nigerian company by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax under the Act.
Where a company's effective tax rate in a year of assessment is less than 15%, it must recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%.

This minimum tax rule applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

gaps: The definition of a small company is not in the passages, so whether the company is small and taxed at 0% cannot be determined.

The company's turnover, whether it belongs to an MNE group, its losses, capital allowances, dividends and other adjustments are needed to find its total profits and whether the minimum tax rule applies.
The question does not say whether the figure is profit before tax or total profits as the Act defines them.
The final tax calculation is not done here.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8 (gazette page A 397)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Section 191(2) of the Nigeria Tax Act says the provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191.

A direction under section 191 is one the relevant tax authority may make where it considers a transaction artificial or fictitious, or a disposition not given effect to; it may disregard the transaction or make adjustments and issue an assessment or additional assessment.

gaps: The passages do not include Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, so they do not show what its objection and appeal provisions say or which body hears them.
The supplied objection and appeal rules are in section 41 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 (in Chapter Two), and the passages do not link them to the Chapter Four reference in section 191.
